As described in the Neuroimaging Methods section, after constructing a representative MBN
for a group of interest with the MS scheme, we correct the adjacency matrix with the FDR and
the Pmap methods, which depend on the threshold α. In data analysis, the p value tends to
decrease when the sample size increases ( Lin et al., 2013 ). Thus, we also investigate the effects
of data imbalance in the construction of MBNs by randomly undersampling and oversampling
the [ 18F]FDG-PET data in our experiments. The random undersampling technique consists in
removing instances from the larger groups until achieving the same size between all groups
(Rodrigues et al., 2017 ). On the contrast, oversampling techniques typically generate synthetic
patterns based on the vicinity of the existing data points, being carried until the smaller groups
approximate the largest group’s size. In this work, we have used the adaptive synthetic sampling
approach for imbalanced learning (ADASYN; He et al., 2008 ) method in our experiments.
Likewise, the construction of more reproducible MBNs tends to be very dependent on the
total number of subjects in a dataset. A great number of subjects produce better estimates of
the underlying distribution of the data, which in turn can be used to construct more reliable
and reproducible MBNs. In our experiments, we also evaluate the effects of the number of
subjects ( ns) as a function of the stability of the MBNs. For these experiments, we perturbed
the MBNs 256 times, set Po 2 [2%, 5%, 8%] and let ns 2 [10, 15, 20, …, 200].
Parameter Tuning
As previously described in the Construction of MBNs 171 Using an MS Scheme section, the
proposed MS bootstrap construction scheme requires as input the number of samples ( n),
which defines the number of different networks that will be constructed to estimate later the
representative matrix of a given group of inte rest. Aiming at optimizing our method, we
assumed that the parameter n was independent of any group, which entails those optimiza-
tions carried out in the space of parameters of one group (e.g., MCI) could be applied to the
other groups (e.g., CU and AD) with no great losses in performance. The adopted optimization
scheme iteratively computed the Bhattacharyya distance (dB) between the degree distribution
(i.e., the normalized histogram of edges connecting paired nodes) of the networks generated
with the MS bootstrap scheme when n = k, against the degree distribution of MBNs generated
when n = k + 100 (with k 2 [100, 200, …, 9900]). We optimized our setup by choosing the
parameter n that minimized the computed dB values.

DISCUSSION
We proposed a novel MS scheme to construct stable MBNs, indexed by an innovative stability
strategy. By applying bootstrap sampling to a dataset of static [ 18F]FDG-PET images, we dem-
onstrated that it is possible to select a representative network from multiple assembled MBNs
that preserve the group ’s characteristics and overall organization. Other frameworks employ-
ing dynamic [ 18F]FDG-PET simultaneously acquired with MRI in hybrid systems have recently
been proposed ( Deery et al., 2024 ; Hahn et al., 2018 ; Reed et al., 2023 ; V olpi et al., 2023).
However, their application remains limited due to the predominance of static [ 18F]FDG-PET
acquisitions in currently available datasets. Additionally, the generated MBN showed greater
resilience to outlier attacks. We introduced a novel thresholding method that leverages the
intersubject variability of the MBNs ’ degree distribution to retain only the connections that
are highly probable among group subjects. Evaluating MBN stability is challenging due to
the absence of a known ground truth, making the definition of a stability criterion inherently
difficult. In this report, we circumvented the issue of defining a unique MBN ground truth for
CU, MCI, and AD groups by expanding on the concept of node attacks ( Albert et al., 2000 )
and introducing an outlier attack model to perturb groups of [ 18F]FDG-PET data, similar to the
approach in Meinshausen and Bühlmann (2010) . This strategy was inspired by previous work
(Rodrigues et al., 2018 ) and aligns with the concept of differential privacy ( Dwork et al., 2015 ),
which holds that a small number of data samples should not significantly affect an algorithm ’s
output. Using the framework proposed by Soundarajan and colleagues, we addressed the
problem of measuring the MBN ’s stability by evaluating the similarity between a group repre-
sentative network and its correspondent perturbed version ( Soundarajan et al., 2014 ). We
tested our method using traditional similarity metrics in the field of pattern recognition. More
specifically, to compare the general similarity between adjacency matrices, we have used the
Frobenius norm and the dH. Additionally, to compare the characteristics of the MBNs, we com-
puted graph theoretical measures and compared the representative MBN with its perturbed ver-
sion in the feature space defined by these graph measures. We used the dE and the dC to assess
similarity, with smaller values indicating greater stability of the MBN.
Notably, we have not found statistically significant differences in the stability measures
between the mean, mode, and median construction criteria. This indicates that the constructed
MBNs may be Gaussian distributed, forming a cluster in a high dimensional manifold. Under
this view, identifying the group representative MBN is equivalent to finding the centroid of this
Gaussian-shaped cluster, which explains why there are no significant differences in the stability
measures between these criteria. It is worth noting that the proposed MS scheme does not rely
specifically on the connectivity measure of choice. Here, for simplicity, we have used the

Pearson correlation measure—which is widely used for constructing MBNs in brain PET imaging
studies—to introduce the overall formalism of this a pproach. Although we used Pearson correla-
tion and tested different thresholding strategies (FDR, Bonferroni, and Pmap), the MS scheme could
be easily adapted to embrace other types of measures and correction methods, such as partial and

information and the maximal information coefficient and other relative thresholding methods using
Z-score, percentile-based, or histogram-based metrics (Reshef et al., 2011). Similarly, the strategy
employed for stability evaluation can be applied regardless of how the adjacency matrices (i.e., the
MBNs) are organized, accommodating different choices of the connectivity measure. Here, we did
not fully explore the vast domain of available similarity measures between matrices in the literature.
The stability results obtained with the MS scheme (see Figures 5–8) revealed a great potential for
assembling stable MBNs, that is, MBNs assembled with the proposed scheme were significantly
more stable than the conventional method. Additional similarity measures could potentially add
information but were not tested here ( Koutroumbas & Theodoridis, 2008).
The results also demonstrated that the MS scheme is robust to the data imbalance issue, show-
ing low variability between the CU, MCI, and AD groups across different scenarios of group
imbalance (ADASYN, Undersampled, and Imbalanced). Indeed, the overall dispersion of each
group is smaller across imbalanced scenarios for the bootstrap MS scheme when compared with
the conventional method. One could argue that the MS scheme may be a proper method for
studying imbalanced datasets from large-scale c linical trials, such as the ADNI cohort. Further-
more, our findings highlight the potential of the bootstrap MS scheme to reduce the number of
individuals required to assemble group representative MBNs withenhanced stability, which could
make MBNs a more widely used secondary outcome in brain PET studies. The computational
burden of the bootstrap approach may be significant in some cases, especially in large-scale
studies or when computational resources are limited. Optimizing the sampling strategy or consid-
ering parallel processing methods could help alleviate this issue and improve computational effi-
ciency. The ADNI and FMUSP data were processed and analyzed independently using different
tools. Nevertheless, the results are similar, which suggests that the method does not depend on the
imaging processing pipeline. In terms of network patterns, we replicated prior findings demon-
strating that MCI and AD brains exhibit a reduction in global metabolic connectivity ( Arnemann
et al., 2017 ; S.-Y . Huang et al., 2020 ; Kuang et al., 2019 ; Pagani et al., 2017 ). Our approach
successfully captures meaningful biological results using a smaller number of participants,
replicating findings from previous studies that used larger sample sizes. This method paves
the way for future studies involving smaller cohorts, enabling the discovery of novel bio-
logical insights. The definitio n and characterization of metab olic networks remain an area
of active debate ( S a l ae ta l . ,2 0 2 3; V ogel et al., 2023 ). These findings highlight the need for
methodological frameworks that account for the unique properties of metabolic imaging,
particularly regarding the relative merits of int ra- versus intersubject approaches. Here, the
MS scheme could offer additional insights into the definition and stability of metabolic net-
works, particularly in the context of group variability. Future applications of these
approaches may help refine metabolic network analysis and improve their integration with
other neuroimaging modalities. Future appli cations of these approaches may help refine
metabolic network analysis and improve the ir integration with other neuroimaging
modalities. In addition, the MS scheme is application-independent, making it suitable
for studying various brain diseases using different measures. It also offers the flexibility
to assemble brain networks derived from multiple PET radiotracers. Moreover, since the
proposed scheme does not depend on data-specific parameters, it could potentially be
applied to other mammalian species, such as nonhuman primates and rodents.

CONCLUSION
In summary, in the present study, we provided a straightforward method to assemble reliable
brain networks with multiple applications in brain PET imaging research. Our method has the
potential to considerably increase PET data reutilization and advance our understating of brain
network dynamics in health and disease.

CAPÍTULO 2

“Metabolic brain network reorganization precedes clinical conversion in Alzheimer’s
disease”
Manuscrito em preparação para ser publicado na revista Alzheimer’s and Dementia.

Este artigo tem por objetivo investigar alterações precoces na organização metabólica
do cérebro associadas à progressão clínica da DA, com foco em indivíduos cognitivamente
saudáveis. Embora o hipometabolismo cerebral medido por PET-FDG seja um marcador bem
estabelecido da doença em estágios sintomáticos, evidências indicam que abordagens
convencionais baseadas em análises tradicionais a nível regional apresentam sensibilidade
limitada nas fases pré-clínicas. Nesse contexto, o presente trabalho adota uma perspectiva de
redes metabólicas cerebrais, permitindo a avaliação da coordenação funcional do metabolismo
da glicose aplicando o método validado no artigo anterior.
Ao integrar dados de PET-FDG com biomarcadores de amiloide e tau ao longo do
continuum da DA, este estudo demonstra que alterações na organização das redes metabólicas
precedem a conversão clínica e ocorrem mesmo na ausência de diferenças detectáveis nos
biomarcadores moleculares clássicos, como PET amiloide e níveis de A b no líquor. Os
resultados sugerem trajetórias divergentes entre indivíduos clinicamente estáveis (que
permanecem cognitivamente saudáveis) e conversores clínicos (que convertem diagnóstico
para comprometimento cognitivo), possivelmente refletindo mecanismos distintos de
vulnerabilidade e resiliência cerebral. Assim, este trabalho contribui para a compreensão dos
mecanismos sistêmicos iniciais da DA e reforça o valor de abordagens baseadas em redes como
ferramentas para a investigação da progressão patológica precoce na doença de Alzheimer.

86
CAPÍTULO 3

“IDO1 genetic variants influence brain glucose metabolism and cognition in living
humans”
Manuscrito finalizado para submissão na revista Science Translational Medicine.

Este artigo corrobora evidências recentes publicadas na revista Science por Minhas et
al. demonstrando que as proteínas Aβ e tau induzem a superexpressão de IDO1 e aumentam
sua atividade em astrócitos, suprimindo a glicólise astrocitária e reduzindo o suporte metabólico
aos neurônios em modelos celulares e animais da doença de Alzheimer (MINHAS et al., 2024).
No entanto, até o momento, não havia evidências demonstrando o impacto da IDO1 sobre o
metabolismo cerebral da glicose e biomarcadores da doença de Alzheimer em indivíduos.
Neste estudo, investigamos o impacto de polimorfismos genéticos da IDO1 sobre o
metabolismo cerebral da glicose, biomarcadores e cognição em uma coorte de 549 indivíduos
cognitivamente saudáveis e com comprometimento cognitivo. Identificamos que portadores de
um haplótipo da IDO1 apresentam hipometabolismo cerebral medido por PET-FDG, atrofia
hipocampal, redução dos níveis de Aβ42 no líquor e pior desempenho em múltiplos domínios
cognitivos. Esses efeitos foram parcialmente mediados por disfunção sináptica e tau. Análises
metabolômicas exploratórias sugeriram alterações no metabolismo do triptofano–nicotinamida
como um possível mecanismo subjacente. Assim, este trabalho contribui para a literatura ao
aprofundar a compreensão do papel da IDO1 na fisiopatologia da doença de Alzheimer e
representa, até onde sabemos, a primeira evidência clínica a corroborar os achados de Minhas
et al.

122
CAPÍTULO 4

“The role of astrocytic glutamate transport via GLT-1 on brain glucose metabolism”
Resultados em preparação.

1. Prefácio
Este projeto experimental foi desenvolvido de forma progressiva ao longo de diferentes
etapas. Entre abril de 2022 e junho de 2023, o projeto foi elaborado e aprovado pelas instâncias
éticas competentes, incluindo a autorização para importação dos animais transgênicos Aldh1l1-
Cre GLT-1 flox. De junho de 2023 a março de 2024, ocorreu a chegada dos animais, a
padronização do protocolo de genotipagem e a expansão das colônias. Entre março e setembro
de 2024, foram obtidos os primeiros animais experimentais, realizada a validação do modelo
de knockdown por meio de tratamento com tamoxifeno e padronizadas culturas primárias de
astrócitos adultos. De setembro a dezembro de 2024, foi estabelecido o protocolo de microPET-
FDG associado à estimulação das vibrissas para ativação do córtex somatossensorial. Entre
janeiro e julho de 2025, iniciaram-se os imageamentos com microPET-FDG, juntamente com
a padronização de ensaios funcionais do GLT -1, imunohistoquímica e experimentos de
reversão do knockdown com ceftriaxona. Por fim, entre agosto e dez embro de 2025, os
experimentos foram temporariamente interrompidos para priorizar a finalização das análises
dos estudos computacionais. Dessa forma, essa seção está apresentada como resultados em
preparação, tendo em vista que é um trabalho ainda em andamento.

130
CAPÍTULO 5

Comentários em revistas científicas

Esse capítulo apresenta dois comentários publicados em revistas científicas. O primeiro
comentário, intitulado “Blood GFAP reflects astrocyte reactivity to Alzheimer’s pathology in
post-mortem brain tissue”, publicado na revista Brain, discute evidências que dão suporte ao
uso do GFAP como um biomarcador periférico da reatividade astrocitária associada à patologia
da DA. O comentário contextualiza os primeiros achados da correlação entre os níveis de GFAP
no sangue com quantificações post-mortem do imunoconteúdo de GFAP em indivíduos com
DA, bem como explora como a ativação de astrócitos se relaciona com a neuropatologia
cerebral e declínio cognitivo (PASCUAL SÁNCHEZ-JUAN et al., 2024). Destacamos as
implicações dos achados de Sánchez-Juan et al. para a compreensão dos mecanismos gliais na
progressão da doença e como podem contribuir na interpretação biológica do uso de
biomarcadores periféricos.
O segundo comentário, intitulado “Assessing brain-wide outcomes of dopamine system
activation in the living rodent brain”, publicado na revista Trends in Neurosciences, aborda
avanços metodológicos no campo da neuroimagem funcional em modelos animais. O
comentário contextualiza a primeira abordagem multimodal em camundongos utilizando
simultaneamente PET-FDG, BOLD-fMRI e ativação optogenética do sistema dopaminérgico
in vivo (HAAS et al., 2024). Discutimos como abordagens integrativas como essa podem
permitir a investigação de questões fundamentais do campo da neuroimagem funcional, como
o acoplamento metabólico e neurovascular. Ademais, enfatizamos como essas técnicas podem
contribuir para uma compreensão mais abrangente da modulação sináptica sobre circuitos
neurais, bem como a interação metabólica entre neurônios e astrócitos.
Em conjunto, os dois comentários apresentam nossa visão sobre como estudos
inovadores nas áreas de biomarcadores da DA e de neuroimagem funcional podem impactar o
campo de pesquisa, enfatizando a importância de compreender a contribuição dos astrócitos
para o funcionamento cerebral em condições fisiológicas e patológicas.

Blood GFAP reflects astrocyte reactivity to
Alzheimer’s pathology in post-mortem brain
tissue
This scientific commentary refers to ‘Serum GFAP levels correlate
with post-mortem brain atrophy and neurofibrillary tangles’ by
Sánchez-Juan et al. (https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/awae035).

Astrocytes, an abundant type of glial cell, undergo molecular, func-
tional and morphological changes in response to pathological stimuli,
a process known as ‘astrocyte reactivity’ or ‘reactive astrogliosis’. The
upregulation of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), the main constitu-
ent of astrocyte intermediate filaments, is a canonical marker of react-
ive astrocytes.1 The notion that GFAP can be released or leaked from
reactive astrocytes to the CSF or blood has formed the rationale for
its use as an astrocyte biomarker in multiple brain disorders including
Alzheimer’s disease. Increases in GFAP levels in Alzheimer’s disease
have consistently been reported in the CSF and, more recently, in
blood using ultrasensitive assays.2 As GFAP is expressed predomin-
antly in astrocytes and these cells are connected to blood vessels,3 it
is intuitive to infer that GFAP’s increased concentration in blood indi-
cates reactive astrogliosis. However, a comprehensive neuropatho-
logical validation is still needed. In this issue of Brain,
Sánchez-Juan
and colleagues4 determine serum GFAP levels in blood samples col-
lected exceptionally close to the post-mortem neuropathological as-
sessment of individuals with dementia. The authors evaluated the
associations between serum GFAP levels and Alzheimer’s disease clin-
ical and neuropathological features and, for the first time, between
serum GFAP and brain tissue GFAP immunostaining.
In a clinicopathological cohort of 139 patients with dementia, ser-
um GFAP levels were measured longitudinally at three time points:
upon admission to a nursing home; at an intermediate point; and
close to post-mortem brain tissue collection. These measurements
were conducted parallel to neuropsychological assessments, brain
MRI scans and post-mortem neuropathological examinations.
Notably, the average interval between brain collection and the latest
blood sampling was 139 days, marking the shortest period reported
in the literature for the neuropathological validation of Alzheimer’s
disease-related blood biomarkers.4 The authors demonstrate a sig-
nificant correlation between pre-mortem serum GFAP levels and
the severity of post-mortem Alzheimer’s disease neuropathology.
Partial mediation models show that serum GFAP levels play a medi-
ator role between brain amyloid and tau, accounting for 49%–57% of
the variance in tau load. These results support the hypothesis that
astrocyte reactivity significantly contributes to the interplay between
amyloid and tau across the Alzheimer’s disease continuum. In a re-
cent multicentre study,5 plasma GFAP levels were found to influence
the association between amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau phosphorylation in
1016 cognitively unimpaired individuals. This observation may
help to explain why certain individuals positive for Aβ in early dis-
ease stages do not exhibit tau accumulation and maintain stable cog-
nitive performance in later stages. These findings highlight the
considerable prognostic potential of blood GFAP.
Sánchez-Juan and colleagues4 also, for the first time, tested the
association between serum GFAP and post-mortem brain GFAP im-
munostaining, with a significant positive correlation being observed
in the superior entorhinal cortex but no association in the amygdala.
One should keep in mind that the number of GFAP-positive astro -
cytes varies greatly across brain regions and, unlike deposits of amyl-
oid and tau, an astrocyte can rapidly change its state from
GFAP-positive to GFAP-negative and vice versa. The regional number
of GFAP-positive astrocytes and the Alzheimer’s disease pathology
load—amyloid plaques and tau tangles—will thus jointly determine
the regional association with blood GFAP concentration. As astro -
cytes continuously undergo state changes,3 blood GFAP levels will
not necessarily correlate strongly with post-mortem GFAP. The read-
er should remember we are dealing with the brain’s homeostatic
cells, which are remarkably plastic. Additionally, astrocyte hetero-
geneity should not be disregarded; one astrocyte may become react-
ive by upregulating GFAP, while another may upregulate monoamine
oxidase-B (MAO-B) instead or as well. Indeed, plasma GFAP and the
astrocyte PET tracer 11C-deuterium-L-deprenyl (11C-DED) signal fol-
low divergent trajectories and may reflect different astrocyte pheno-
types in Alzheimer’s disease.6 To add more complexity, the biological
response of GFAP-positive astrocytes to amyloid is remarkably dis-
tinct from the response to tau.7
Sánchez-Juan and collaborators 4 also found a negative correl -
ation between serum GFAP levels and cognitive performance in
the severe Mini-Mental State Examination (sMMSE) test.
Furthermore, serum GFAP levels were significantly elevated in
Alzheimer’s disease dementia cases, showing approximately a
2-fold increase at both initial and final collection time points.
These heightened serum GFAP levels effectively distinguished neu-
ropathologically confirmed Alzheimer’s disease dementia from
non-Alzheimer’s disease dementia cases, as evidenced by a re -
ceiver operator characteristic analysis area under the curve of
0.91 upon admission. Additionally, in a longitudinal analysis, indi-
viduals with a higher burden of Alzheimer’s disease pathology at
the time of death exhibited higher levels of serum GFAP at baseline.
Unlike that observed for tau or amyloid biomarkers, serum GFAP

seemed not to plateau but instead continued to increase until the
premortem examination. The fact that serum GFAP strongly corre-
lates with Alzheimer’s disease neuropathology is noteworthy, but it
is unlikely that its performance as a diagnostic biomarker would be
superior to blood phosphorylated tau epitopes. 8 However, blood
GFAP could definitely play a role as a prognostic biomarker in
Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders.
Astrocytes exert a notable influence on the pathophysiology of nu-
merous brain disorders, contributing either positively or negatively to
clinical outcomes, via gain or loss of astrocytic functions. These com-
plex responses may differ over the course of disease spatiotemporal
progression.1 For example: (i) blood GFAP is a US Food and Drug
Administration-approved biomarker for detecting individuals with
traumatic brain injury (TBI) and abnormalities on head CT scans. 9
Therefore, through a GFAP blood test, individuals with suspected TBI
can bypass unnecessary expenses and exposure to CT radiation; and
(ii) in a large-scale blood proteomic study involving 52 645 individuals
without dementia at baseline, GFAP emerged as a highly specific pre-
dictor for dementia, encompassing Alzheimer’s disease, incident all-
cause dementia and vascular dementia, more than 10 years prior to
diagnosis. It is worth noting that individuals with elevated GFAP levels
were 2.9 times more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease compared to
those with lower baseline GFAP levels.10 The lack of disease specificity
of blood GFAP changes should not be interpreted as a limitation but as
a strength, since it could serve as a useful screening biomarker. More
specifically, a GFAP-positive blood test could be interpreted as a non-
specific signal of neurodegeneration, highlighting the need for add-
itional confirmatory testing and further clinical examinations.
The Alzheimer’s Association workgroup is proposing GFAP as a
biomarker of inflammation and a marker of ‘astrocyte activation’ in
their revised diagnostic criteria. While it is unlikely that GFAP could
play a role as a diagnostic biomarker, it would definitely provide use-
ful information as a predictive or prognostic biomarker, as shown by
Sánchez-Juan and colleagues’4 demonstration that blood GFAP levels
are negatively correlated with cognitive performance and that indivi-
duals with higher GFAP levels at baseline had earlier disease onset.
This important work reinforces the idea that blood levels of GFAP
can play a role in tracking astrocyte reactivity. The fact that blood
GFAP reflects Alzheimer’s disease clinical and neuropathological se-
verity highlights the intricate role of astrocytes as the homeostatic
cells of the brain ( Fig. 1). The astrocytic continuum in Alzheimer’s
disease and other neurodegenerative disorders could even be the ‘sil-
ver bullet’ that helps us to understand why some people with high le-
vels of pathology do not progress to clinical stages. The field has been
dominated by protein aggregates and biomarkers of neurodegenera-
tion; it is now time to embrace the heterogeneous response of astro-
cytes as a very promising biomarker target.

Assessing brain-wide
outcomes of dopamine
system activation in the
living rodent brain
Christian Limberger1 and
Eduardo R. Zimmer 1,2,3,4,5, *
In a recent study, Haas, Bravo, and
colleagues integrated optogenetic
stimulation with simultaneous
functional in vivo positron emis-
sion tomography (PET)/magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) mea-
surements in rats. By activating
the nigrostriatal pathway in the
substantia nigra pars compacta
(SNc), they observed concurrent
metabolic and hemodynamic ﬂuc-
tuations associated with the dopa-
minergic pathway in living animals
at the whole-brain level.
Trends in Neurosciences, Month 2024, Vol. xx, No. xx
Brain circuits refer to networks of neurons
that work together to process information
and regulate various brain functions, from
basic survival mechanisms to complex cog-
nitive tasks. These circuits are governed by
neurotransmitter communication systems
within neurons and other brain cells, which
interact by exchanging signals, metabolites,
and substrates, thereby altering their state
and energy demands [1]. The dopaminergic
system is a critical neuromodulatory system
in the human brain, having important roles in
motor control, reward processing, cognitive
functions, and emotional regulation [2]. Al-
though multiple techniques have been
used to study the circuitry of the dopaminer-
gic system, little is known about this circuitry
in the living brain at the whole-brain level.
In a recent publication, Haas, Bravo, and
colleagues [ 3] performed simultaneous
blood oxygen level-dependent functional
MRI (BOLD-fMRI) and functional PET
(fPET) with [18 F]2-ﬂuor-2-deoxy-d-glucose
(FDG) in rats under optogenetic stimulation
of the dopaminergic system (Figure 1). Dur-
ing stimulation of the nigrostriatal pathway
in the right SNc, the authors simultaneously
measured brain glucose metabolism and
hemodynamic responses (changes in oxy-
genated blood ﬂow), revealing the energetic
and vascular responses to dopaminergic
system manipulation in living rats.
The authors found low positive BOLD sig-
nal changes in multiple areas of the basal
ganglia on the ipsilateral side, followed by
a robust BOLD signal overshoot after the
termination of the optogenetic stimulation
in ipsilateral regions. Interestingly, negative
BOLD signal changes appeared in the con-
tralateral side in multiple areas, such as the
striatum, nucleus accumbens, amygdala,
and S1. To directly compare hemodynamic
and metabolic responses, the authors eval-
uated the FDG-fPET signal. There was an
increase in glucose metabolism during op-
togenetic stimulation in multiple ipsilateral
areas, including the substantia nigra, mid-
brain, thalamus, hypothalamus, and stria-
tum. However, no negative signal changes
were found on the contralateral side.
Haas, Bravo, and colleagues then evaluated
the overlap of activated voxels from BOLD-
fMRI and FDG-fPET, providing an elegant
whole-brain map of hemodynamic and met-
abolic responses to the activation of the
nigrostriatal pathway. Although some over-
lap is present, the authors captured the un-
coupling of hemodynamic and metabolic
responses to SNc stimulation. These results
reinforce early canonical ﬁndings indicating
uncoupling between cerebral blood ﬂow
and oxidative metabolism during brain re-
gional activation by somatosensory stimula-
tion [ 4] and recently investigated using
hybrid PET/MRI technology in humans [5].
One of the strengths of in vivo brain imaging
is that one can identify regional differences,
sometimes even more so if combined
with selective stimulation techniques,
such as optogenetics. The dynamic ﬂuc-
tuations captured by these imaging
techniques allowed identiﬁcation of an
interesting activation/inhibition control
mechanism, which Haas, Bravo, and col-
leagues propose is related to the inhibition
of dopamine release [3]. This control mech-
anism limits the BOLD signal during stimu-
lation. When stimulation ends, the inhibition
is lifted, causing a signal overshoot. Inter-
estingly, in the striatum, the BOLD-fMRI
activation maps showed greater spatial
extension compared with fPET, whereas
the substantia nigra exhibited the opposite
pattern. This ﬁnding suggests that inhibition
of neuronal activity in the SNc during
optogenetic stimulation is a metabolically
demanding process characterized by in-
creased regional glucose metabolism.
Supporting this, higher c-fos expression
was observed in the dorsal striatum,
which receives input from the SNc, while
no changes were detected in the SNc itself,
despite the high metabolic demand during
stimulation [3].
Further functional and molecular connectiv-
ity analyses revealed a metabolically active
isolation mechanism in regions receiving do-
paminergic input triggered by optogenetic
stimulation. This phenomenon appears to
functionally isolate the right striatum from
areas upstream in the nigrostriatal pathway,
which may be linked to the axonal projec-
tions of dopaminergic neurons from the
substantia nigra that co-release dopamine
and GABA [3]. These ﬁndings illustrate the
intricate interaction of metabolic and hemo-
dynamic processes, moving beyond the
simplistic interpretation of brain-region acti-
vation [6]. Given that astrocytes are contrib-
utors to the signal of BOLD-fMRI [ 7] and
FDG-fPET [ 8] imaging modalities, the ap-
proach of simultaneous in vivo metabolic
and hemodynamic evaluation may contrib-
ute to a better understanding of the cooper-
ation between neurons and other brain cells.

in the elegant study by Haas, Bravo, and

(BOLD-fMRI) and functional positron emission tomography (fPET) with [ 18 F]2-ﬂuor-2-deoxy-
d-glucose (FDG) under optogenetic stimulation of the dopaminergic system enables the
simultaneous in vivo assessment of metabolic and hemodynamic alterations. A recent study by Haas,
Bravo, and colleagues [ 3] combined optogenetic stimulation with simultaneous functional PET/MRI imaging in
living rats. Their multimodal setup revealed the effects of nigrostriatal pathway activation on brain energy
metabolism and blood ﬂow at the whole-brain level. The authors demonstrated an uncoupling mechanism
between metabolic and hemodynamic responses. An immediate increase in the BOLD signal was observed on
the same side of stimulation, whereas negative BOLD signal changes appeared in the contralateral side in
multiple brain areas, such as the striatum, nucleus accumbens, amygdala, and S1. In the striatum, the BOLD-
fMRI activation maps showed greater spatial extension compared with FDG-fPET. This suggests that inhibition
of neuronal activity in the substantia nigra pars compacta during optogenetic stimulation is a metabolically active
process, characterized by increased regional glucose consumption. The experimental approach followed by the
authors has the potential to bring novel insights into the relation between oxygen consumption and glucose
metabolism in response to the activation of speciﬁc brain circuitries.

4. CONCLUSÕES

Esta tese de doutorado foi dedicada à compreensão das alterações metabólicas cerebrais
associadas à DA. Inicialmente, desenvolvemos um novo método para a construção de redes
metabólicas cerebrais a partir de exames de PET-FDG. Em seguida, aplicamos esse método à
investigação de alterações pré-clínicas da doença. Por fim, avaliamos como polimorfismos
genéticos na IDO1 podem influenciar o metabolismo cerebral da glicose em indivíduos com
DA.
No Capítulo 1, descrevemos o desenvolvimento e a validação de um novo método para
a construção de redes metabólicas cerebrais derivadas de PET-FDG. Demonstramos que essa
abordagem é capaz de capturar a organização da atividade metabólica cerebral de forma mais
estável e reprodutível, mesmo com amostras menores, superando limitações metodológicas de
abordagens convencionais baseadas exclusivamente em covariância metabólica.
No Capítulo 2, aplicamos esse método para investigar alterações metabólicas pré -
clínicas da DA em indivíduos cognitivamente saudáveis. Os resultados indicaram que
trajetórias de estabilidade cognitiva e de conversão para comprometimento cognitivo estão
associadas a diferenças na arquitetura das redes metabólicas cerebrais, e não a padrões regionais
isolados de captação do FDG, reforçando o valor das redes como arcabouço teórico para
investigação de teorias moleculares da propagação neuropatológica da DA.
No Capítulo 3, exploramos a influência de variantes genéticas da IDO1 sobre o
metabolismo cerebral da glicose. Identificamos associações entre polimorfismos da IDO1 e
hipometabolismo cerebral em regiões vulneráveis à DA, bem como pior desempenho cognitivo
e maior declínio longitudinal, sugerindo que vias moduladas pela IDO1 podem contribuir para
a heterogeneidade da progressão da DA.
No Capítulo 4, estabelecemos e validamos um modelo experimental para investigar o
papel dos astrócitos na regulação do metabolismo cerebral da glicose, sobretudo sua
contribuição para o sinal do PET-FDG. Padronizamos um modelo de knockdown específico do
transporte glutamatérgico astrocitário em camundongos transgênicos Aldh1l1-Cre GLT-1 flox,
criando uma plataforma translacional para o estudo de mecanismos celulares que conectam
disfunção astrocitária e metabolismo energético.
No Capítulo 5, discutimos, em dois comentários científicos, como avanços recentes em
biomarcadores da DA e em neuroimagem funcional têm potencial para redefinir a nossa área
de pesquisa, ressaltando a importância de estudar e compreender o papel central dos astrócitos
em estados fisiológicos e patológicos, por meio de diferentes abordagens.

138
Sob uma perspectiva conceitual, esta tese contribui para a consolidação de uma mudança
de paradigma na interpretação do metabolismo cerebral da glicose na DA. Ao invés de ser
tratado apenas como um marcador tardio de neurodegeneração neuronal, o metabolism o
energético cerebral emerge neste trabalho como um fenômeno sistêmico, dinâmico e integrador,
sensível a alterações moleculares, genéticas, celulares e de organização em redes que se
manifestam ainda nas fases mais iniciais da DA. Essa visão amplia o escopo explicativo dos
biomarcadores metabólicos e os reposiciona como elementos centrais na compreensão da
fisiopatologia da doença.
Do ponto de vista metodológico, o desenvolvimento de um novo pipeline para a
construção de redes metabólicas cerebrais a partir de PET -FDG representa uma inovação
relevante para a área de neuroimagem. A abordagem proposta responde a limitações
reconhecidas da literatura, como a dependência de grandes amostras, a instabilidade das redes
baseadas exclusivamente em covariância metabólica e a baixa reprodutibilidade entre estudos.
Ao permitir a caracterização robusta da organização metabólica cerebral mesmo em amostras
reduzidas, o método amplia a viabilidade de estudos longitudinais e pré -clínicos, os quais
geralmente apresentam reduzido tamanho amostral. Além disso, o método pode ser aplicado
para outros radiotraçadores além do FDG, ampliando a reutilização de dados de neuroimagem
amplamente disponíveis e subutilizados na literatura.
O estudo das redes metabólicas em indivíduos cognitivamente saudáveis reforça a
relevância do método como um potencial biomarcador sensível de vulnerabilidade pré-clínica.
Os resultados demonstram que trajetórias distintas de progressão clínica estão assoc iadas à
arquitetura das redes metabólicas cerebrais, e não apenas a alterações regionais isoladas de
captação do FDG. Esses achados fortalecem as hipóteses do envolvimento das redes cerebrais
na progressão da DA e oferecem um elo entre teorias moleculares da propagação
neuropatológica, como a cascata amiloide e a disseminação da tau, e alterações em larga escala
a nível de rede. Assim, as redes metabólicas cerebrais passam a ser compreendidas não apenas
como reflexo da doença, mas como potenciais mediadoras da sua progressão.
A identificação de associações entre variantes genéticas da IDO1, hipometabolismo
cerebral e declínio cognitivo acrescenta uma dimensão mecanística e integrativa ao estudo da
DA. Ao conectar genética, imunometabolismo e função cerebral, esta tese contribui para
explicar parte da heterogeneidade clínica observada na doença e reforça o papel de vias
imunometabólicas como moduladoras da vulnerabilidade individual. Esses achados são
particularmente relevantes no contexto atual da pesquisa em DA, que busca ultrapassar modelos
unidimensionais e incorporar abordagens de investigação multimodal.

139
A validação de um modelo experimental de knockdown astrocitário do transportador
GLT-1 representa um avanço importante para a área, ao permitir a investigação causal do papel
dos astrócitos na regulação do metabolismo cerebral da glicose e na contribuição do sinal do
PET-FDG. Esse modelo supre uma lacuna crítica na literatura, pelo potencial de poder dissociar
contribuições neuronais e gliais para alterações metabólicas observadas in vivo, e estabelece
uma plataforma translacional robusta para testar hipóteses derivadas de estudos clínicos e
computacionais.
Em conjunto, os resultados desta tese posicionam o metabolismo cerebral da glicose
como um eixo central de integração entre processos moleculares, celulares e de rede que se
manifestam precocemente na DA. Ao articular abordagens computacionais inovadoras,
investigações clínicas em humanos e validação experimental em modelos animais, este trabalho
oferece contribuições originais e complementares que avançam o estado da arte da área. Além
de gerar conhecimento fundamental, os achados apresentados fornecem bases conceituais e
metodológicas sólidas para o desenvolvimento futuro de biomarcadores prognósticos sensíveis
às fases iniciais da doença e para a proposição de estratégias terapêuticas precoces voltadas à
modulação do metabolismo cerebral e da função glial na DA.
